relationship: bodily collapse and burning faces amid terror
rationale: Nahum combines broken hearts, loosening knees, pains at the waist and faces like a scorching pot. Isaiah likewise describes slackened hands, cowardly souls, labor pains and faces changed as to flame. Both gather bodily weakness, pains and fiery facial imagery to describe terror.
source_text: Shaking out, tossing up and boiling over; broken hearts, loosening knees, pangs at every waist, and every face like the scorching of a pot.

target_units.text: Therefore every hand will slacken, and every human soul grow cowardly;
the envoys will be troubled, and labor pains will hold them like those of a woman giving birth. They will lament to one another and be distraught, and change their face as to flame.

relationship: ruling power pictured as lions and cubs
rationale: Nahum asks where the lions' dwelling and cubs' pasture have gone. Ezekiel introduces a lament over Israel's ruler with a mother among lions and her cub becoming a prey-seizing lion. Both present political power through a lion family, in different national settings.
source_text: Where is the lions’ dwelling and the pasture that belonged to the cubs, where a lion went to enter there, a lion’s cub, and no one frightened them?

target_units.text: “And you, take up a lament over Israel’s ruler,
and say: What was your mother? A cub! She came to be among lions; among lions she multiplied her cubs.
One of her cubs sprang away; he became a lion, learned to seize prey, and ate human beings.

relationship: a lion's predation pictures destructive rule
rationale: Nahum's lion fills its nest with prey and dwelling with plunder for its young. Ezekiel likewise depicts a lion learning to seize prey, eating people and desolating cities. Both apply predatory lion behavior to destructive power.
source_text: A lion seized enough for his cubs and strangled for his lions; he filled his nest with prey and his dwelling with plunder.

target_units.text: He moved among lions, became a lion, learned to seize prey, and ate human beings.
He fed in his boldness, desolated their cities, and destroyed the land and its fullness by the sound of his roaring.

relationship: the ending of a lion's power and audible activity
rationale: Nahum announces the destruction of lions and prey, after which the addressed one's deeds will not be heard again. Ezekiel likewise describes nations capturing the lion and imprisoning him so his voice will not be heard on Israel's mountains. The lion image ends in removal in both, with different stated actions silenced.
source_text: Look, I am against you, says the Lord Almighty. I will burn your multitude in smoke; the sword will consume your lions. I will destroy your prey from the earth, and your deeds will never again be heard.

target_units.text: Nations from the surrounding countries set themselves against him and spread their nets over him; he was caught in their destruction.
They put him in a muzzle and a cage. He came to Babylon’s king, and he brought him into prison, so that his voice would not be heard upon Israel’s mountains.

relationship: a city accused of bloodshed and lawlessness
rationale: Nahum addresses a city of bloodshed, falsehood and injustice. Ezekiel likewise commands judgment of the city of bloodshed and displays its lawless deeds, blood and defilement. Both frame the city's coming judgment through an explicit bloodshed accusation.
source_text: O city of bloodshed, wholly false, full of injustice! Prey will not be touched.

target_units.text: “And you, son of man, will you judge the city of bloodshed? Display all her lawless deeds to her,
and say, ‘Thus says the Lord, the Lord: O city shedding blood within her so that her time may come, making reflections against herself to defile herself!

Through their blood that you shed you have transgressed, and through your reflections that you made you were being defiled. You brought your days near and brought the season of your years. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all the countries

relationship: the sound of horses announces a destructive approach
rationale: Nahum describes the sounds of whips, wheels, a pursuing horse and a jolting chariot within the attack scene. Jeremiah likewise makes the sound of horses and their neighing herald an attacker who devours a city and its inhabitants. Both evoke an assault through the sound of its horses.
source_text: The sound of whips and the sound of shaking wheels, of a pursuing horse and a jolting chariot,

target_units.text: From Dan we will hear the shrill sound of his horses; at the sound of the neighing of his riding horses the whole earth shook. And he will come and devour the earth and its fullness, a city and those dwelling in it.

relationship: multitudes of slain in a judgment against nations
rationale: Nahum's mounted attack culminates in a multitude of slain and a grievous fall. Isaiah likewise announces wrath against nations, handing them to slaughter, with wounded and dead thrown out. Both describe mass casualties within judgment upon nations.
source_text: and of a mounting horseman, a flashing sword and glittering weapons, a multitude of slain and a grievous fall! There was no limit to her nations, and they will weaken in their bodies

target_units.text: For the Lord’s wrath is against all nations, and anger against their number, to destroy them and hand them over to slaughter.
Their wounded and dead will be thrown out; their odor will rise, and mountains will be soaked with their blood.

relationship: a powerful city accused of prostitution and sorcery
rationale: Nahum describes the city as a prostitute and mistress of potions, selling nations and tribes through these practices. Isaiah addresses Babylon with accusations of prostitution, sorcery and enchantments before its destruction. Both combine these accusations against a personified city, without equating every alleged action.
source_text: because of the multitude of prostitution. A prostitute, beautiful and pleasing, mistress of potions, selling nations through her prostitution and tribes through her potions,

target_units.text: Now these two will come upon you suddenly, in one day: widowhood and childlessness will come suddenly upon you, amid your sorcery and the overwhelming power of your enchanters,

in your hope of wickedness. For you said, ‘I am, and there is no other.’ Know that understanding these things and your prostitution will become your shame. You said in your heart, ‘I am, and there is no other.’

Destruction will come upon you, and you will certainly not know it—a pit, and you will fall into it. Misery will come upon you, and you will certainly not be able to become clean. Destruction will come upon you suddenly, and you will certainly not know it.
Stand now amid your enchantments and your abundant sorcery, which you learned from youth, if you can be helped.

relationship: a personified city's shame is exposed
rationale: Nahum announces exposed hind parts, shame shown to nations and dishonor to kingdoms. Isaiah likewise commands Babylon to uncover and declares that her shame and reproaches will become visible. Both present public exposure as the humiliation of a city figured as a woman.
source_text: look, I am against you, says the Lord God Almighty. I will expose your hind parts over your face and show nations your shame and kingdoms your dishonor,

target_units.text: Take a millstone and grind flour. Uncover your veil, expose your gray hair, pull up your garments to bare your lower legs, and cross rivers.
Your shame will be uncovered, and your reproaches will be visible. I will exact justice from you; I will certainly no longer hand it over to humans.”

relationship: defilement leads to public disgrace before other peoples
rationale: Nahum announces abomination cast upon the city according to its impurities and its being made an example. Ezekiel likewise links defilement and bloodshed to the city becoming a reproach and mockery among nearby and distant countries. Both describe public disgrace associated with the city's impurities.
source_text: and cast abomination upon you according to your impurities, and make you an example,

target_units.text: Through their blood that you shed you have transgressed, and through your reflections that you made you were being defiled. You brought your days near and brought the season of your years. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all the countries
near you and far away from you. They will mock you: “Unclean, the famous one, abundant in lawless deeds!”

relationship: passersby react to Nineveh's devastation
rationale: Nahum describes everyone seeing miserable Nineveh springing away and questioning who will lament her. Zephaniah likewise names Nineveh's wasteland and describes passersby hissing and waving their hands. Both make onlookers' responses part of the same named city's humiliation.
source_text: and everyone seeing you will spring away and say, “Miserable Nineveh! Who will lament her? Where shall I seek consolation for her?”

target_units.text: He will stretch His hand against the north and destroy the Assyrian, making Nineveh a waterless wasteland like a wilderness.

Flocks and all the wild animals of the earth will graze within her; chameleons and hedgehogs will lie in her recessed panels. Wild animals will cry in her openings, and ravens in her gateways, for cedar is her structure.

This is the contemptuous city dwelling in confidence, saying in her heart, “I am, and there is no one after me.” How she became a wasteland, pasture for wild animals! Everyone passing through her will hiss and wave his hands.

relationship: Egypt, Ethiopia and Libyan support within announced defeat
rationale: Nahum names Ethiopia and Egypt as strength and Libyans as helpers in the account of Amon. Ezekiel likewise groups Egypt, Ethiopia and Libyans in a sword judgment and says Egypt's supports will fall. The named network of support connects the passages without identifying all their cities or events.
source_text: and Ethiopia was her strength, and Egypt, and there is no limit to the flight; Libyans became her helpers.

target_units.text: A sword will come upon the Egyptians, and there will be turmoil in Ethiopia; wounded men will fall in Egypt, and her foundations will collapse together.
Persians, Cretans, Lydians, Libyans, all the mixed company, and some of the sons of My covenant will fall by the sword in her.
Egypt’s supports will fall, and the arrogance of her strength will come down from Migdol to Syene; they will fall in her by the sword, says the Lord.

relationship: infants dashed to the ground amid a city's defeat
rationale: Nahum describes the addressed city's deportation, infants dashed down and nobles bound. Hosea likewise announces Samaria's disappearance, sword deaths and nursing infants dashed to the ground. The particular violence against infants is shared, with different cities named.
source_text: She too will go into deportation as a captive; they will dash her infants to the ground at the head of all her roads, cast lots for all her glorious things; and all her nobles will be bound in handcuffs.

target_units.text: Samaria will disappear because she opposed her God. They will fall by the sword; their nursing infants will be dashed to the ground, and their pregnant women will be ripped open.

relationship: a defeated city portrayed as drunken
rationale: Nahum says the addressed city too will become drunk and seek a place away from enemies. Isaiah describes Jerusalem drunk from the Lord's cup of anger and promises that cup to its oppressors. Both portray a city's affliction through drunkenness, with Isaiah explicitly identifying its cup imagery.
source_text: You too will become drunk and be overlooked; you too will seek a place to stand away from enemies.

target_units.text: Awake, awake, rise, Jerusalem, you who drank the cup of anger from the Lord’s hand. You drank out and emptied the cup of falling, the bowl of anger.
There was no one to comfort you among all your children you bore, and no one to take your hand among all your sons you raised.
These two confront you—who will grieve with you?—fall and crushing, famine and sword. Who will comfort you?
Your sons are helpless, sleeping at every way out like a half-boiled beet, full of the Lord’s anger, exhausted because of the Lord God.
Therefore listen, humbled one, drunk but not from wine.
Thus says the Lord God who judges His people: ‘Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of falling, the bowl of anger. You will not drink it again.
I will throw it into the hands of those who wronged and humbled you, who told your soul, “Bend down, so we may pass.” You laid your back level with the earth, outside for passersby.’”

relationship: a vulnerable object of judgment compared to a readily eaten fig
rationale: Nahum compares fortresses with fig trees that fall into the eater's mouth if shaken. Isaiah likewise compares fallen glory with an early fig that a viewer wants to swallow immediately. The fig-eating image portrays how readily what seemed substantial can be consumed.
source_text: All your fortresses are fig trees having lookouts; if shaken, they will fall into the eater’s mouth.

target_units.text: The flower fallen from the hope of glory, on the high mountain’s summit, will be like an early fig: whoever sees it will want to swallow it before taking it into his hand.

relationship: defenders compared with women and defensive bars destroyed
rationale: Nahum says the people are like women, the gates open to enemies and fire consumes bars. Jeremiah likewise describes Babylon's crushed warriors becoming like women, dwellings burned and bars shattered. The linked military simile and ruined defenses closely connect the defeat scenes.
source_text: Look, your people within you are like women! The gates of your land will open wide to your enemies, and fire will consume your bars.

target_units.text: Babylon’s warrior has ceased fighting; they will sit there in confinement. Their power was crushed; they became like women. Her dwellings were burned; her bars were shattered.

relationship: water supplies and fortifications prepared for siege
rationale: Nahum commands drawing siege water and holding fortresses while working mud, straw and brick. Isaiah describes water diverted into the city, walls strengthened and water provided between walls. Both describe practical defensive preparations, without assigning identical building materials to the passages.
source_text: Draw water for yourself for the siege, hold your fortresses firmly; step into mud, be trampled in straw, hold fast over the brick.

target_units.text: and uncover the hidden things of the houses in David’s citadel. They saw that they were many and that the old pool’s water had been diverted into the city,
and that Jerusalem’s houses had been pulled down to fortify the city’s wall.
You provided water for yourselves between the two walls, inside the old pool, and did not look to the One who made her from the beginning or see the One who founded her.

relationship: locust devouring used to portray destruction
rationale: Nahum describes fire and sword consuming the city and compares devouring with a locust. Joel names successive caterpillar, locust, bruchus and blight devouring what remains. The shared connection is destructive devouring by locusts; Nahum expressly applies it as a comparison.
source_text: There fire will consume you; a sword will destroy you, devouring you like a locust, and you will become heavy like a crawling locust.

target_units.text: What the caterpillar left, the locust devoured; what the locust left, the bruchus locust devoured; what the bruchus locust left, the blight devoured.

relationship: same-chapter flight represented by locusts
rationale: Nahum 3:16 follows multiplied trading with a crawling locust rushing out and flying away. The next verse likewise depicts a mixed company leaping away like locusts when the sun rises. The repeated insects' departure develops the chapter's image of disappearing strength.
source_text: You multiplied your trading beyond the stars of heaven. A crawling locust rushed out and flew away.

target_units.text: Your mixed company leaped away like a young locust, like a locust perched on a fence on frosty days. The sun rose, it leaped away, and it did not know its place. Woe to them!

relationship: same-chapter recurring locust departure
rationale: The mixed company in 3:17 leaps away like a locust and no longer knows its place. The preceding verse pictures a crawling locust rushing out and flying away after the reference to multiplied trade. Both use locust departure to expose what does not remain.
source_text: Your mixed company leaped away like a young locust, like a locust perched on a fence on frosty days. The sun rose, it leaped away, and it did not know its place. Woe to them!

target_units.text: You multiplied your trading beyond the stars of heaven. A crawling locust rushed out and flew away.

relationship: people scattered on mountains without effective shepherds
rationale: Nahum describes slumbering shepherds, rulers put to sleep and people departed upon mountains with no one receiving them. Micaiah likewise sees Israel scattered on mountains like a flock without a shepherd. Both portray the people dispersed without leadership, in different national settings.
source_text: Your shepherds slumbered; the Assyrian king put your rulers to sleep. Your people departed upon the mountains, and there was no one receiving them.

target_units.text: Micaiah said, “Not so! I have seen all Israel scattered on the mountains like a flock without a shepherd. The Lord said, ‘These have no master. Let each return to his own house in peace.’”

relationship: Nineveh's fall draws a hostile public response
rationale: Nahum ends with hearers clapping over the news of the addressed power's incurable wound because of its continual evil. Zephaniah names Nineveh's devastation and passersby hissing and waving hands. Both depict public reaction to the arrogant city's ruin, while Nahum explicitly gives its widespread evil as the reason.
source_text: There is no healing for your crushing; your wound has become inflamed. All who hear the report of you will clap their hands over you, for upon whom has your evil not continually come?

target_units.text: He will stretch His hand against the north and destroy the Assyrian, making Nineveh a waterless wasteland like a wilderness.

Flocks and all the wild animals of the earth will graze within her; chameleons and hedgehogs will lie in her recessed panels. Wild animals will cry in her openings, and ravens in her gateways, for cedar is her structure.

This is the contemptuous city dwelling in confidence, saying in her heart, “I am, and there is no one after me.” How she became a wasteland, pasture for wild animals! Everyone passing through her will hiss and wave his hands.
